scores.evidence: Keyword search matters for error codes, feature names and SKUs, which embeddings handle poorly.
scores.rationale: Technical claims (hybrid search rationale, pgvector adequacy at <10k articles, embedding-change-forces-reindex, cross-encoder reranking) are accurate and precisely state real limits.

scores.evidence: Non-goals for v1: account-specific actions (refunds, password resets), multi-turn troubleshooting flows, and anything that needs the customer's own data.
scores.rationale: Covers all core implied capabilities, resolves ambiguities with stated assumptions and open questions, and explicitly justifies exclusions with a realistic phased path.

scores.evidence: Store metadata per article: article_id, title, url, section/category, product, plan_tier, locale, updated_at, visibility
scores.rationale: Data flows connect end-to-end (metadata captured at ingestion is used for filtering, citation and conflict resolution), error paths route consistently to escalation, with no contradictions.

scores.evidence: Regression gate: run the eval in CI for any change to prompts, chunking, models or the index. Block a release if a metric drops.
scores.rationale: Eval set built before tuning from real tickets, targets labeled as starting points, adversarial cases included, calibrated LLM-judge, agent-assist pilot before customers, and continuing online metrics.

scores.evidence: I don't know your stack, doc platform or volume yet, so this plan is vendor-neutral and lists its assumptions.
scores.rationale: Assumptions and estimates are explicitly flagged, baselines are measured before targets, and the open questions state which answers change which concrete choices.

scores.evidence: Made-up policies or prices | Strict grounding prompt, grounding check, always escalating on billing or legal topics
scores.rationale: The major domain failures (hallucination, stale docs, bot loops, injection, wrong plan/version) have concrete detection and mitigation, but LLM-provider outages, retries and partial pipeline failures are unaddressed.

scores.evidence: monitor ingestion lag and alert if an updated article isn't re-indexed within N minutes
scores.rationale: Observability, freshness alerting, versioning and a weekly review loop are concrete and team-sized, but deployment/rollback mechanics are implicit and operational ownership is left as an open question.

scores.evidence: cache answers to frequent questions (invalidate when the source article changes), set token budgets, and rate-limit per session
scores.rationale: Inference as the cost driver is implicitly recognized with concrete controls and model-tier trade-offs, but there is no per-conversation cost estimate or discussion of how costs scale with traffic.

scores.evidence: version the prompts, embedding model and chunking config. Changing the embedding model means a full re-index.
scores.rationale: The costly-to-reverse choices (embedding model, index, prompts) are versioned and validated early via the eval gate, and vendor neutrality limits lock-in, though explicit exit paths are thin.

scores.evidence: For help-center scale (usually under 10k articles), pgvector or OpenSearch is plenty.
scores.rationale: Simplest workable design with speculative additions explicitly marked optional, scale sized to the actual domain, and nothing essential omitted; complexity like reranking is justified by need.

scores.evidence: 0. Discovery | 1 wk | Doc inventory, ticket analysis (top intents), golden set v1, metric baselines
scores.rationale: Phased build order with dependency-justified sequencing (eval before tuning, agent-assist before customers), checkable gates per phase, and decisions specific enough to start immediately.

checklist.evidence: use a CMS webhook on publish, update or delete, plus a nightly full reconciliation. Deletes must remove chunks from the index.
Chunk by document structure (H2/H3 sections)... Store metadata per article: article_id, title, url, section/category, product, plan_tier, locale, updated_at, visibility
Golden dataset (200–500 questions): take them from real historical tickets and chat logs... run the eval in CI for any change
Answer only from the provided context. Cite article URLs. If the context doesn't contain the answer, say so and offer escalation.
create a ticket with the full transcript, the retrieved articles, and the bot's draft answer, so agents don't start from zero
treat retrieved text and user text as data, not instructions. The bot should have no tools that can take actions in v1.
Exclude internal-only articles, drafts... Filter on article visibility metadata... Metadata filters: locale, product, and plan tier (if known from the session)
redact card numbers, SSNs and similar data before logging. Set a log retention policy.
Non-goals for v1: account-specific actions (refunds, password resets)... These come later, through tools or APIs.
Weekly review: sample about 50 conversations, look at failures, and fix the cause. Most fixes will be doc gaps
cache answers to frequent questions (invalidate when the source article changes), set token budgets, and rate-limit per session

traps.evidence: Answer only from the provided context. Cite article URLs. If the context doesn't contain the answer, say so and offer escalation.
Exclude internal-only articles, drafts, and anything with agent-only notes. Filter on article visibility metadata.
use a CMS webhook on publish, update or delete, plus a nightly full reconciliation. Deletes must remove chunks from the index.
run the eval in CI for any change to prompts, chunking, models or the index. Block a release if a metric drops.
For help-center scale (usually under 10k articles), pgvector or OpenSearch is plenty.

note: A near-exemplary RAG plan that avoids all the classic traps with eval-first discipline and proportionate design; its only notable gaps are missing cost-per-conversation quantification, thin PII/retention/provider-terms specifics, and unaddressed provider-outage handling.
